items.title: I finally self-hosted my passwords, and it's simpler than I expected
items.author: Yash Patel
items.content: I’ve been making small changes to my workflow lately, mostly by replacing tools I’ve relied on for years with simpler alternatives. I enjoy experimenting with open-source apps and self-hosted software because they give me more control while often fitting better into the way I work. Still, there was one change I had kept putting off. I had thought about making it several times, but always found a reason to leave things as they were. Recently, I finally decided to stop procrastinating and make the switch. It turned out to be one of those changes that makes your workflow feel simpler almost immediately.

items.title: This open-source productivity toolkit solved my context switching problem without adding complexity
items.author: Yash Patel
items.content: I used to think context switching was just part of working on a computer. I'd move from one task to another, check something quickly, and then try to get back into the zone. The problem was that those small interruptions started adding up. I wanted a simpler way to stay focused without building another complicated productivity system. That's when I came across Koncentro, an open-source app that took a different approach to managing my work.

items.title: It took me a year to find a real Pocket replacement, and it was self-hosted the whole time
items.author: Yash Patel
items.content: I was genuinely annoyed when Pocket disappeared because it was one of those apps I never thought much about until I no longer had it. I tried different apps that promised to fill the gap, but most felt too complicated or lacked the simplicity I wanted. Eventually, I stopped looking at the usual cloud-based options and started exploring what was available in the self-hosted world. That's when I came across Karakeep.

items.title: HUANUO's back-to-school sale brings huge discounts to ergonomic desk upgrades
items.author: Sponsored
items.content: Back-to-school season is not just about pencil cases and laptops anymore. For a lot of families, it is also the point in the year when the desk setup gets a rethink, whether that is a student settling into hybrid classes, a teacher prepping lesson plans at home, or a parent working remotely while managing the household schedule.

items.title: I gave up on Obsidian twice before I found the setup that finally stuck
items.author: Nolen Jonker
items.content: Not every app you try works the first time. I have hundreds installed and often find myself stumbling onto an old one that I'd written off too soon, only to realize it's actually fantastic. Sometimes all it takes is a different setup, or perhaps different life circumstances that now require a curated stack. Notes apps fall into this category too, especially Obsidian.

items.title: 4 tiny open-source tools that save me hours every week
items.author: Victor Awogbemila
items.content: After years of working with various tools designed to make my writing process faster and more efficient — including both paid and free ones — I've found out that, for obvious reasons, paid versions are often the best overall. But before you toss free software into your recycle bin, hear me out.

items.title: This Immich fork does what Google Photos still can't
items.author: Dhruv Bhutani
items.content: Switching over to Immich was one of the best self-hosting decisions I made. It gives me the convenience of Google Photos while giving me full ownership of my data by running on my NAS. It's got all the essential features like face recognition, albums, and search, and it works well enough that I don't need to look elsewhere. But as good as it is, Immich isn't perfect.

items.title: The best productivity tool I set up this month is built for developers, and I should have done it sooner
items.author: Nolen Jonker
items.content: Every productivity app I've written about this year has more or less the same vibe and rhythm to it. You usually download and install it, then before it does anything useful, you have to pick a template or set up some type of system first. And I think this upfront tax is the reason why so many productivity tools end up unused after the first weekend.

items.title: I turned Obsidian into a full project manager by adding one folder to my vault
items.author: Nolen Jonker
items.content: It's no secret that Obsidian vaults can get pretty messy, and I'm especially prone to that. This is amplified even more by the fact that I have three separate vaults. And with every new one, I tell myself this is going to be the one I stay on top of, but somehow just end up in the same place. My attempts at trying to keep things organized show up with the little folders scattered here and there, but I just end up with a long list of unfiled notes at the root.

items.title: Microsoft Loop is an underrated productivity gem that you are not using
items.author: Parth Shah
items.content: Microsoft Loop started off as yet another Notion clone on the market. However, ever since the launch, the Windows maker has done a solid job with frequent updates, and thanks to a few neat add-ons, it even surpasses some of the best productivity tools in the market. While many of us are still stuck juggling multiple apps to stay organized, Loop offers a simple, more cohesive way to work.
